ruststream-amqp is the AMQP 1.0 broker for RustStream, built on the fe2o3-amqp client. AMQP 1.0 is an ISO standard, so one crate serves the whole family: ActiveMQ Artemis and Classic, RabbitMQ 4.x, Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs, Amazon MQ, Solace, Apache Qpid and IBM MQ. On RabbitMQ, AMQP 1.0 is a separate protocol stack from the 0.9.1 that ruststream-lapin speaks.
This section draws how AMQP 1.0 works, where ruststream-amqp sits between the broker and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.

AMQP 1.0 joins two containers by one connection, which carries sessions, and each session carries links that move messages one way. The service presents the container id ruststream unless container_id names another, and a broker's console lists the service's connection and links under it. The connection is one TCP socket. On an amqps:// URL it starts with TLS. SASL then authenticates the service with PLAIN, ANONYMOUS or EXTERNAL, and the two containers exchange open. A session is a pair of channels inside the connection, each with a window that bounds the transfers in flight on it. The crate begins one session that every publisher of the connection shares, and one more for each subscription. A slow subscription fills its own window, never the publishers' one or another subscription's. A link is named and carries messages in one direction. A sender link goes from the service to a node, and a receiver link from a node to the service. Each end of a link is a terminus, and the terminus on the broker's side names a node by its address. A link also has a credit of its own, which Transfers draws. The standard fixes the frames on the wire, not what an address means. Whether orders is a queue or a topic is the broker's decision, which Addresses draws. The model is the specification's (transport, security).

An address names a node in the broker, and the capability a receiver asks for decides whether its receivers share a queue or each get a copy. AmqpAddress::queue asks for the capability queue, AmqpAddress::topic for topic, and AmqpAddress::raw for none. ActiveMQ Artemis reads the capability. With queue, the receivers of an address attach to one anycast queue and compete: each message goes to one of them. With topic, the address is multicast and Artemis gives each receiver a subscription queue of its own, so each receives every message. Artemis creates an address and its queues on the first attach unless its settings forbid it, and orders::billing names one queue of an address directly. A topic subscription keeps the terminus defaults of the specification: not durable, and expiring with its session. Its subscription queue lives as long as the link, so what is published to the topic while the service is stopped is not kept for it. A raw address reaches the broker exactly as written, and the broker's own configuration decides what it is. Other brokers address their nodes in their own way: RabbitMQ 4 names a queue /queues/orders and an exchange /exchanges/events/key, and the queue must exist beforehand. Azure Service Bus names a queue by its name and a topic subscription events/subscriptions/billing. A receiver may ask for a dynamic source instead of naming one. The broker then creates a node, Artemis a temporary queue, and returns its address in its answer to the attach. request attaches one such receiver for every request, sends the address in reply-to, and detaches the receiver when the reply has arrived or the timeout has passed. The terminus fields are the specification's (messaging, section 3.5), and the address model is Artemis's (AMQP, address model).

An AMQP 1.0 transaction is declared at the broker's coordinator, and the transfers posted under it reach their nodes together on the commit or not at all. A controller link attaches to it and sends declare, and the coordinator answers with a transaction id. A transfer on any ordinary sender link then carries that id in its transactional state. discharge ends the transaction: with fail false it commits, and with fail true it rolls back. AmqpTxnPublisher posts under a transaction. Each begin_transaction and each owned transaction attaches a controller link of its own on the connection's publisher session and declares one transaction, and commit and abort discharge it. Several transactions are open on one connection at a time, and Artemis keeps them apart. The controller asks for the mixed sender settle mode, because Artemis answers with that mode and the client requires the broker to echo the one it asked for. Brokers differ here. RabbitMQ 4 does not support AMQP 1.0 transactions. Azure Service Bus supports them, and posts to several entities in one transaction through a send-via entity. The protocol is the specification's (transactions), and the broker limits are each vendor's (Artemis, RabbitMQ, Service Bus).

A sender transfers a message only against the receiver's link credit, and the receiver settles each one with a disposition that carries its outcome. Link credit over time: the receiver grants it, the sender spends it, and the client grants a new window once half has been settledReceiver: the serviceSender: the brokerflowtransferhalf settledflowflowlink-credit 256transfersup to the creditdispositionsfor 128 deliveriesflowlink-credit 256 againtransferscontinueCredit counts transfers from the last flow:a delivery the service still holds does not return it The diagram as text Receiver: the service: flow link-credit 256; dispositions for 128 deliveries; flow link-credit 256 again Sender: the broker: transfers up to the credit; transfers continue flow link-credit 256 → transfers up to the credit: flow transfers up to the credit → dispositions for 128 deliveries: transfer dispositions for 128 deliveries → flow link-credit 256 again: half settled flow link-credit 256 again → transfers continue: flow Credit counts transfers from the last flow: a delivery the service still holds does not return it Credit is the receiver's flow control. The receiver sends a flow frame with a credit, and the sender may make that many transfers before it waits for the next one. A subscription grants 256 by default, and credit sets another count. The fe2o3-amqp client manages the credit itself. Each time half of the credit has been settled, it grants the full credit again, counted from the transfers received so far. So the sender never runs dry while the service works, and it never runs more than one window ahead of the last grant. Its outcome is one of four. accepted finishes the message. rejected calls it invalid, and the broker's dead-letter policy decides what happens to it. released returns it untouched, and the next delivery carries the same delivery-count. modified with delivery-failed returns it as a failed attempt, and the next delivery counts one more. undeliverable-here on modified asks the broker not to deliver it to this receiver again. delivery-count lives in the message's header section and counts the earlier attempts that failed. Brokers differ on modified: Artemis counts it, RabbitMQ 4 supports it on quorum queues only, and Azure Service Bus does not use it. The flow control and the settle modes are the specification's (transport, sections 2.6.7 and 2.8), and so are the outcomes (messaging, section 3.4).

How ruststream-amqp measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real broker, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on AMQP 1.0.

One process runs the scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. An fe2o3-amqp receiver, driven directly: receive, decode, read a field, accept. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, the address descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the connection, the session each link rides, the link credit of 256, the delivery guarantee, the place of the ack, the decode into the same struct, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. The body is 512 bytes of JSON. It decodes into a struct of two integer fields, so the decode allocates nothing and the number is about this crate rather than about the JSON parser.

A fresh address per run. A run never sees what an earlier one left. The consumer attaches first. A producer on a second connection then feeds it, at most 8192 messages ahead. It publishes them pre-settled, so the run measures the consuming side rather than how fast the broker confirms a send. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is decoded, in all three loops. Connecting, beginning the sessions and attaching the links are outside it. The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when the consumer spent most of the run waiting on the broker. That is arithmetic: a probe times 20000 sends that wait for their disposition and takes the median, the transport states how many round trips one delivery costs, and the row is flagged when their product reaches half the measured time per message. A delivery here costs none: the broker transfers against credit the client tops up in the background, and an accept is sent without waiting for an answer. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, on AmqpBroker against the same broker, built without the testing feature and run on a single-threaded runtime. A thread of its own, on another connection, fills the queue between the measured regions, and every one of its publishes waits for the broker to accept it. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. The socket is real, so a count moves a little between runs of one binary: how many transfers one read brings in depends on what the broker had written by then. A run against a saved baseline fails on two percent more instructions in a scenario. Allocations are held to a floor each scenario declares, the highest count seen plus a tenth of a percent, on every run.

just bench The recipe starts the stand from docker-compose.test.yml, runs the comparison, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes about a minute and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count takes about half a minute and needs valgrind. The recipe installs the benchmark runner itself, at the release the lock file pins. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-amqp measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, on one broker. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. Another AMQP 1.0 broker would move all three figures of a row together, which is why the broker's image is published with them. The broker runs on the same machine, on the loopback. With no network latency, the same cost per message is a larger share of the time than it would be against a broker across a network. Read the percentage as an upper bound on what a deployed service pays. A negative difference is the read-ahead, not a saving of the code: the crate's subscription keeps receiving while the loop above it works, and the raw loop does not. A broker-bound row is one where the consumer waited on the broker for most of the run. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside that wait, and the difference comes out near zero. That is a lower bound on the cost, not a measurement of it.

documents.t: An instruction count holds this crate's code, the runtime above it and the fe2o3-amqp client's work on the service's thread. It moves a little between runs, because the broker is real. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Connecting, attaching and the first allocations behind them are the cold start, paid once.

A row is one consumer reading one queue address, a small body and a single broker. It measures what a delivery costs inside this crate, not what the broker can carry. The comparison measures the consuming side only. What a publish costs on the service's thread is the reply row of the code chart. Throughput of publishing is bounded by the broker's round trip, because a publish waits for its disposition, as Path draws. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

The runtime above it is the same for every broker. What is particular to AMQP 1.0 is in this crate: the address descriptor, what an ack means, where a retry copy goes and how a transaction posts. A connected broker holds one connection. Its publishers share one session, and the first publish to an address attaches a sender link that every later publish to that address reuses. The connection owns those links, so a shutdown can close each one and wait for the broker's answer. Each subscription begins a session of its own and attaches one receiver link on it. Subscriptions and their sessions start on the runtime the broker connected on, whichever thread opens them. A handler on a thread of its own therefore leaves no part of the connection on that thread. The crate opens the TCP socket itself, with Nagle's algorithm off. A publish and a request each send a small frame and wait for the answer, which is the pattern Nagle's algorithm delays until the peer's acknowledgement. A message carries no envelope of the framework's own. The well-known headers ride the properties section, the partition key as group-id, and every other header rides application-properties. A message from another AMQP client arrives with its headers, and one this crate sent reads as a plain AMQP message. The asyncapi feature describes the addresses with x-ruststream-amqp1 objects, because the specification reserves its amqp1 bindings and leaves them empty. How the pieces start and stop is on Lifecycle, and the way of one message on Path.

With the testing feature, TestApp::start connects the same broker to an in-process transport instead of a server. The descriptors, the policies and the deliveries are the production ones, and a publish goes through the same conversion into AMQP sections. It routes by exact address: the queue receivers of an address compete, and each topic subscription gets a copy. A queue subscription creates its queue, which keeps a message until a receiver takes it. It settles in the subscription's mode, counts a modified delivery in delivery-count, returns an unsettled delivery to the queue when its subscription detaches, and answers a request over a private reply address. A transaction publishes nothing before its commit. What is the server's own is left to a live run: link credit, how a server creates an address a publish reaches first, the dead-letter policy behind a rejection, the server's own delivery limit and durability. In process a message to an address no queue subscription has attached to is dropped, and a raw address is delivered once, where Artemis may fan it out. Without the feature the transport is not compiled. A production build's connected broker is one shared pointer to the connection, and the compiler checks that size.

The way of one AMQP 1.0 delivery through a RustStream service: the pump, the channel, the handler, the reply and the disposition. The path of one delivery that is answered, from the broker's transfer to its dispositiontransferon the subscription's receiver linkPump task: Receiver::recvheaders from the properties sections,bytes from the data sectionBounded channelas deep as the link creditDispatchone loop, or a lane per keyDecodefrom the delivery's bytesHandlerasync fn under #[subscriber]Replyencoded into the loop's bufferAmqpPublisherholds the address's sender linkuntil the broker's dispositionSettlementa command back to the pump taskdispositionaccepted, modified or rejected The diagram as text transfer on the subscription's receiver link → Pump task: Receiver::recv headers from the properties sections, bytes from the data section Pump task: Receiver::recv headers from the properties sections, bytes from the data section → Bounded channel as deep as the link credit Bounded channel as deep as the link credit → Dispatch one loop, or a lane per key Dispatch one loop, or a lane per key → Decode from the delivery's bytes Decode from the delivery's bytes → Handler async fn under #[subscriber] Handler async fn under #[subscriber] → Reply encoded into the loop's buffer Reply encoded into the loop's buffer → AmqpPublisher holds the address's sender link until the broker's disposition AmqpPublisher holds the address's sender link until the broker's disposition → Settlement a command back to the pump task Settlement a command back to the pump task → disposition accepted, modified or rejected A subscription's pump task owns its receiver link. Receiving needs the link to itself, while a settlement only reads it, and the delivery a handler holds has to travel between tasks. So the pump receives, and every settlement comes back to it as a command. The client's answer returns to the handler through a slot the subscription reuses, so a settlement allocates nothing. The pump turns a transfer into an AmqpMessage. The headers come from the properties and application-properties sections, the bytes from the data section, and delivery-count from the header section. Several data sections read as their bytes joined in order. A string or binary value section is read as bytes too, and any other body, a sequence body included, is rejected and reported to the subscription. The pump then puts the delivery in a channel as deep as the link credit, and settles commands while it waits for room there. A delivery the client cannot read, such as one larger than the link allows, is reported and the link stays attached. A broker that transfers past the credit it was given breaks the link, and the subscription ends. The handler's reply is encoded into a buffer the dispatch loop reuses. The AmqpPublisher takes that buffer as the message's data section, without a copy. It sends the message unsettled on the address's sender link and holds the link until the broker's disposition arrives. So the publishes to one address from one connection go out one at a time, each one round trip. A disposition other than accepted is an error. A reply that fails to publish acks the delivery and reaches the handler's .error continuation with the broker's error. The delivery settles after the reply. Its outcome becomes a disposition, as Settlement draws.

The parts of ruststream-amqp an AMQP 1.0 service uses, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to. The broker, AmqpBroker, holds the connection. A subscription names its address with a descriptor, and a handler's outcome becomes the delivery's disposition. A service publishes through a policy, asks another service with request-reply, and posts several messages as one transaction. The AMQP bindings describe the service in its AsyncAPI document, and a TestApp test runs it on an in-process transport.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document says AMQP 1.0: the protocol key amqp1, and the crate's facts under the x-ruststream-amqp1 extension. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. The specification has an amqp1 binding, and every one of its objects must stay empty. So this crate writes what it knows into one extension object, x-ruststream-amqp1, at each level where the binding would sit. A server names the protocol and the container the service presents. A channel names its node address and, for a subscription, the link it reads over. A send operation says how it posts. A reply routed per request says where its address is read. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors and the publish policies. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-amqp = { version = "0.8", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label amqp, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example amqp_asyncapi --features asyncapi,transaction -- asyncapi gen prints the document. A subscription's channel reports its address, terminus, credit and settle mode; a publish channel reports the address its sender targets. A subscription's extension has four fields, read from its AmqpAddress. address is the node the receiver attaches to. capability is the terminus it asks for, queue or topic. An AmqpAddress::raw address asks for none, so its channel has no capability. credit is the link credit, 256 unless the descriptor sets credit. settleMode is at-least-once, or at-most-once for a descriptor with SettleMode::AtMostOnce. A channel the service publishes to carries one field, address: the node the sender attaches its target to. That is a reply destination, the name of an Out slot, or a dead-letter address. A reply routed per request has no fixed address on its channel, and the extension still names the destination its mount site declared.

The channel orders reports a queue with a credit of 64, events a topic settled at most once, and /queues/audit no terminus. The channels receipts, orders.dead and ledger report the address each sender targets. Macros Manual examples/amqp_asyncapi.rs #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders").credit(nonzero!(64)), reply("receipts"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::topic("events").settle(SettleMode::AtMostOnce))] async fn watch(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "event seen"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::raw("/queues/audit"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/amqp_asyncapi.rs /// The queue `orders`, with a credit of 64. fn orders() -> AmqpAddress { AmqpAddress::queue("orders").credit(nonzero!(64)) } /// The topic `events`, settled on receipt. fn events() -> AmqpAddress { AmqpAddress::topic("events").settle(SettleMode::AtMostOnce) } /// The address `/queues/audit`, sent as written. fn audit_queue() -> AmqpAddress { AmqpAddress::raw("/queues/audit") }

A send operation says how it posts: confirmed for Publish, transactional for TransactionalPublish. The extension of a send operation has one field, posting, and the publish policy at its mount site decides it. Publish posts confirmed: each transfer waits for the broker's outcome, and anything but accepted fails the publish. TransactionalPublish posts transactional: the transfers carry a transaction and become visible at its commit. A dead-letter destination has a send operation of its own, and it posts confirmed. A reply has no send operation. What a reply policy adds to the document is on its reply.

The operation send_events_orders_dead posts confirmed, and send_payments_ledger posts transactional. A reply reports $message.header#/reply-to as where its address is read, so a transform can answer each request where it asked. A request on this broker sets the AMQP reply-to property, and a handler reads it as the reply-to header. A reply can follow it: a transform on out_reply that declares Destination = Names sets the reply's address from that header. The reply then has no fixed address, and the receive operation's reply says where a client reads it: $message.header#/reply-to. Both publish policies report that location. The mount site still names a reply destination, such as reply("receipts"). It is the reply's declared channel, and a delivery the transform leaves alone, one without reply-to, is answered there.

The reply of receive_orders reports its address location as $message.header#/reply-to. Macros Manual examples/amqp_asyncapi.rs /// The receipt names no address of its own, so the transform may name one per delivery. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// Answers where the request asked to be answered: the `reply-to` property, which a handler reads /// as the `reply-to` header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] struct ToReplyTo; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToReplyTo { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(address) = cx.headers().get_str("reply-to") { let address = address.to_owned(); out.set_name(address); } } } examples/manual/amqp_asyncapi.rs /// The receipt names no address of its own, so the transform may name one per delivery. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// Answers where the request asked to be answered: the `reply-to` property, which a handler reads /// as the `reply-to` header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)] struct ToReplyTo; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToReplyTo { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(address) = cx.headers().get_str("reply-to") { let address = address.to_owned(); out.set_name(address); } } }

The server reports the host and port with protocol amqp1 and version 1.0, the container id, and never the credentials in the URL. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the broker's URL. The user and the password the URL carries stay out of it. The protocol is amqp1, and protocolVersion is 1.0. The specification's key amqp means AMQP 0.9.1, and both protocols use the amqp:// scheme and port 5672. The key and the version tell a reader, or a tool that generates a client, which protocol the service speaks. The extension carries containerId, the name the service presents on the connection. It is the broker's container_id, ruststream when the service sets none. An operator finds the service's links by that name in the broker's console.

The broker's URL carries a password, and the server in the document is broker.example.com:5672 with the container billing-svc. Macros Manual examples/amqp_asyncapi.rs /// The production broker. AmqpBroker connects a service to an AMQP 1.0 broker; new only records the URL, and the runtime connects it once at startup. AMQP 1.0 is an ISO standard, so one broker type serves ActiveMQ Artemis and Classic, RabbitMQ 4.x, Azure Service Bus, Amazon MQ, Solace, Apache Qpid and IBM MQ. AmqpBroker::new takes the broker's URL: amqp://host:port, or amqps://host:port for TLS. A URL without a port uses 5672 for amqp and 5671 for amqps. The constructor does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: the authentication and the container id. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedAmqpBroker. The connect opens the socket, authenticates and opens the AMQP connection, so a broker that is unreachable or refuses the service fails startup instead of the first publish. Every subscription and every publisher of the service runs on that one connection. At shutdown the runtime closes the connection, and the connected form is consumed with it. #[subscriber("orders")] opens the address orders as it is written, without a terminus capability. The broker's own configuration then decides whether the subscriptions on the address compete or each get a copy. AmqpAddress::queue and AmqpAddress::topic state that choice in the service; the Subscriptions pages describe them. Getting started runs a first service against a local ActiveMQ Artemis.

The service reads the queue address orders. cargo run --example amqp_service --features testing -- run starts it against a broker on localhost:5672 with the user artemis. container_id names the service to the broker, which is how an operator finds its links in the broker's console; the default is ruststream. Every AMQP 1.0 connection opens with a container id, the name of the process on each end. Each link the service attaches takes its name from it, with a role and a number that keeps the name unique on the connection: Link Name a subscription's receiver <container>-receiver-<n> a publisher's sender, one per address <container>-sender-<n> the reply link of a request <container>-reply-<n> the controller of a transaction <container>-txn-<n> The generated AsyncAPI document reports the container id beside the server's host and port, in the x-ruststream-amqp1 extension.

The service presents itself to the broker as orders-svc. AmqpError is the one error type of the crate: connect, session, attach, publish, a header with no property form, receive, request, transaction and a body with no bytes. Each variant names the step that failed. The client's error behind it is its source, so the fe2o3-amqp types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the URL, the socket, TLS, the login or the AMQP open failed, or the connection failed to close at shutdown Session the broker refused a session, the publishers' or a subscription's Attach the broker refused a link: a subscription's receiver, a publisher's sender, a request's reply link Detach a link failed to close at shutdown Publish the connection failed while a message was sent PublishNotAccepted the broker settled a published message as rejected, released or modified, so the message is not on the broker UnsupportedHeader a header that rides the properties section has a value its property cannot hold: reply-to or the partition key that is not UTF-8, a content-type that is not ASCII; the message is not sent Receive the connection failed while a subscription received UnsupportedBody a delivery's body is an AMQP value that is neither binary nor a string, or a sequence; the delivery is rejected, and the runtime logs the error RequestTimeout a request had no reply within its timeout NotConnected a publisher, a subscription or a transaction was used before the connect or after the shutdown InvalidAddress a subscription's address is empty Transaction a transaction step was called in a state that cannot serve it (transaction feature) A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as a source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it as the source of the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. A publish refused before the message leaves hands the message back with the error: NotConnected, UnsupportedHeader, and an Attach of the publisher's sender link. Once the client sends the message it owns it, so a Publish or PublishNotAccepted refusal carries none. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

The handler sends each shipment to the warehouse address its order names. A shipment the broker refuses drops the order, since sending it again meets the same answer; any other failure retries it. Macros Manual examples/amqp_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(warehouses): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = warehouses .message(&shipment) .to(order.warehouse.as_str()) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not sent"); if refused_by_the_broker(&err) { HandlerOutcome::drop() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } } /// Whether the broker settled the message with an outcome other than accepted. Sending it again /// meets the same answer, while a connection that failed under the publish may be back by the next /// attempt. fn refused_by_the_broker(err: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> bool { let mut cause = Some(err); while let Some(err) = cause { if let Some(AmqpError::PublishNotAccepted { .. }) = err.downcast_ref() { return true; } cause = err.source(); } false } examples/manual/amqp_broker_errors.rs struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .to(order.warehouse.as_str()) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not sent"); if refused_by_the_broker(&err) { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// Whether the broker settled the message with an outcome other than accepted. Sending it again /// meets the same answer, while a connection that failed under the publish may be back by the next /// attempt. fn refused_by_the_broker(err: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> bool { let mut cause = Some(err); while let Some(err) = cause { if let Some(AmqpError::PublishNotAccepted { .. }) = err.downcast_ref() { return true; } cause = err.source(); } false }

One glob, ruststream_amqp::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, the descriptor and the policies under Publish and TransactionalPublish. use ruststream_amqp::prelude::*; is the one import an AMQP 1.0 service writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome, Out and nonzero! come with it. It adds AmqpBroker with its authentication Sasl, the address descriptor AmqpAddress with its delivery guarantee SettleMode, the crate's error AmqpError, and the capability trait RequestReply. The publish policies come under the names every broker crate uses: Publish is AmqpPublish, and with the transaction feature TransactionalPublish is AmqpTransactionalPublish, next to the capability trait TransactionalPublisher. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on these names; the prefixed originals, exported here too, tell them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher> or Out<impl RequestReply>, and names no broker type. A service that reads a delivery's partition key through the Partitioned capability imports ruststream::Partitioned itself. In the glob it would make partition_key() ambiguous with the method of the same name that the core prelude brings.

The broker, its authentication, the descriptor with its settings and the reply policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/amqp_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_amqp::prelude::*; #[subscriber( AmqpAddress::queue("orders") .credit(nonzero!(64)) .settle(SettleMode::AtLeastOnce), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://broker.internal:5672").sasl(Sasl::anonymous()), |b| b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish), ) } examples/manual/amqp_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_amqp::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://broker.internal:5672").sasl(Sasl::anonymous()), |b| { let confirm = subscriber( AmqpAddress::queue("orders") .credit(nonzero!(64)) .settle(SettleMode::AtLeastOnce), Confirm, ); b.include(confirm.reply().build()).out_reply(Publish) }, ) }

Sasl picks the authentication: anonymous, plain or external; an amqps:// URL needs the rustls or native-tls feature, and Tls sets the trusted authorities and the client certificate. A service logs in one of two ways, and a broker uses one of them. Credentials in the URL, amqp://user:password@host, log in with SASL PLAIN. A profile set with sasl goes with a URL that carries no credentials: Profile Login Sasl::plain(user, password) SASL PLAIN with the user and password as written Sasl::anonymous() SASL ANONYMOUS, for a broker that admits clients without credentials Sasl::external() SASL EXTERNAL: the broker takes the identity of the client certificate; it needs an amqps:// URL and the certificate A password the deployment hands the service, from the environment or a secret store, goes through Sasl::plain. So does a password with a character the URL reserves, such as @, :, / or %. A connection with neither credentials nor a profile opens without SASL, and a broker that requires a login refuses it. A refused login, such as a wrong password, and Sasl::external on an amqp:// URL fail startup with AmqpError::Connect. An amqps:// URL encrypts the connection with TLS. The handshake starts as soon as the socket opens, which is what a broker's TLS port expects. The rustls feature checks the broker's certificate against the Mozilla root certificates built into the binary. The native-tls feature uses the operating system's TLS library and its trust store; with both features enabled, native-tls is the one used. The connect checks the certificate against the host in the URL, so the URL names the broker by a host name or an IPv4 address. An IPv6 address gives TLS no server name, so the connect fails on it. AmqpBroker::tls takes the connection's TLS settings, a Tls value: Setting What it does root_certificates(pem) Trusts the certificate authorities in the PEM, beside the default ones client_identity(certificate, key) Presents the client certificate, proven by its PKCS #8 key Every setting is PEM text the deployment hands the service. The settings are read when the broker connects, so a PEM that does not parse fails startup. TLS settings on an amqp:// URL fail startup too: that connection would go out in the clear. Neither the certificates nor the key appear in the broker's Debug output or the generated document. A TestApp test reads the URL as the connect reads it, so an amqps:// URL without a TLS feature fails startup there too. The test does not read the certificates, so it runs without the deployment's. The login itself happens only against a broker, in a live test. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and port and never the credentials in the URL. Connecting to production takes the URL and the credentials from the environment.

The dependency line: ruststream-amqp = { version = "0.8", features = ["rustls"] } The service logs in as orders-svc over TLS. The password comes from the environment. The dependency line is the same. The service logs in with SASL EXTERNAL, and the broker takes its identity from the client certificate. The broker's own authority verifies the broker. Macros Manual examples/amqp_broker_security.rs /// The broker at `url`, logging in with the client certificate: the broker's authority, and the /// service's certificate and key, all PEM. fn certificate_broker(url: &str, ca: &str, certificate: &str, key: &str) -> AmqpBroker { let tls = Tls::new() .root_certificates(ca) .client_identity(certificate, key); AmqpBroker::new(url).tls(tls).sasl(Sasl::external()) } examples/manual/amqp_broker_security.rs /// The broker at `url`, logging in with the client certificate: the broker's authority, and the /// service's certificate and key, all PEM. fn certificate_broker(url: &str, ca: &str, certificate: &str, key: &str) -> AmqpBroker { let tls = Tls::new() .root_certificates(ca) .client_identity(certificate, key); AmqpBroker::new(url).tls(tls).sasl(Sasl::external()) }

Shutdown ends the subscriptions, the publisher links and the connection in turn; a publisher used afterwards reports AmqpError::NotConnected. When shutdown begins, the runtime stops reading and waits for the handlers still running. The app's shutdown_timeout bounds that wait; without it the runtime waits until every handler has finished. A publish returns once the broker has settled the message, so what the handlers published is on the broker by then, and nothing is left to send. The broker then closes from the inside out: each subscription's session ends, the publishers' sender links detach, their shared session ends, and the connection closes. Each layer still has to carry the broker's answer to the layer inside it, which fixes the order. The connection closes only after every subscription's session has ended, the sessions of subscriptions still open at shutdown included, so a clean stop reports no error. Every step runs even after an earlier one fails, so a stuck link cannot leave the connection open. The shutdown reports the first failure in that order: AmqpError::Detach for a link, AmqpError::Session for the session, AmqpError::Connect for the connection. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it, or a transaction begun on a transactional publisher, returns AmqpError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection. A delivery settled after the shutdown reports an error, and the stream of a subscription that was still open ends.

Handlers still running at shutdown get ten seconds to finish before the broker closes. Macros Manual examples/amqp_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Once shutdown begins, the handlers still running get ten seconds to /// finish before the broker closes. fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place)) .shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672")) } examples/manual/amqp_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Once shutdown begins, the handlers still running get ten seconds to /// finish before the broker closes. fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| { let place = subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue(orders()), Place); b.include(place.build()) }) .shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672")) }

Startup opens the socket, authenticates and begins the publishers' session; a refusal fails the start as AmqpError::Connect. The runtime connects the broker once, before any handler runs. The connect opens a TCP socket to the URL's host with Nagle's algorithm off: AMQP sends a small frame and waits for the answer, which that algorithm would hold back. Over the socket it runs TLS for an amqps:// URL, the SASL login, and the AMQP open with the service's container id. It then begins one session that every publisher of the service shares. A failure of the socket, TLS, the login or the open fails startup with AmqpError::Connect, and a session the broker refuses with AmqpError::Session. The service exits before it reads anything. Each subscription then begins a session of its own and attaches a receiver link to its address. AMQP counts flow control per session, so a slow subscription holds back neither the publishers nor another subscription. An attach the broker refuses fails startup with AmqpError::Attach, which names the address. An empty address fails with AmqpError::InvalidAddress before any I/O. A publisher attaches its sender link to an address on the first publish there, and every later publish to the address reuses that link. A TestApp test connects in process and reads the URL as the connect reads it. A scheme other than amqp or amqps, a URL without a host, or amqps without a TLS feature fails startup in a test as in production. A refused socket or login happens only against a broker, in a live test.

AmqpPublish, Publish in the prelude, waits for the broker's disposition and reports anything but accepted as PublishNotAccepted. The policy has no fields, so a mount site writes it bare. It is named wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish) for retry copies. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into an AmqpPublisher. It is also the broker's default policy, so a reply registration that names no policy publishes through it. The publishers share one AMQP session. A sender link is attached to an address on its first publish and kept for the next ones. Each publish waits for the broker's outcome of the transfer. An accepted outcome completes it; rejected, released or modified fails it with the address and the outcome, so a refusal never passes as sent. The message carries the encoded value as one data section. Headers ride the message's properties and application-properties sections, and the partition key rides group-id. A publish carries no per-message settings: the message goes out without the header section, so it is not durable and keeps the default priority and no time to live. Where a reply goes is a property of its type: #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] fixes the address. A reply to an address the request names is the request-reply pattern.

content-type, correlation-id, reply-to and message-id ride the AMQP properties section; every other header rides application-properties. The crate adds no envelope of its own, so a peer that does not use RustStream reads a plain AMQP message. On publish each well-known header fills the property of the same name. The partition key fills group-id. Any other header becomes an application property: a UTF-8 value as a string, any other value as binary. A property takes a value only in a form it holds, so a header that rides one travels unchanged or fails the publish. reply-to and the partition key are strings and take UTF-8. content-type is a symbol and takes ASCII. message-id and correlation-id go as a string when the value is UTF-8 and as binary otherwise. A value outside its property's form fails the publish with AmqpError::UnsupportedHeader, which names the header and the address. On delivery a handler reads both sections as one header map, through ctx.headers(). correlation_id() and reply_to() read the two properties request-reply uses; a responder reads the correlation in its own type with Ctx<ReplyCorrelation>. A message id or a correlation id the sender wrote as a string or binary reads as its bytes; one written as a UUID reads as its hyphenated hex, and a number as its decimal digits. An application property reads in a form that keeps its value, though not its AMQP type: Sender wrote Header value a string or a symbol its UTF-8 bytes binary its bytes a boolean, a number or a char its text, which parses back to the same value a timestamp milliseconds since the epoch, as text a UUID its hyphenated lowercase hex null an empty value a decimal its IEEE 754 bytes a described value its AMQP encoding A message type declares its headers with #[outgoing(headers = ..)], and a field renamed to correlation-id lands in the property. A HeaderMap with the same entries works the same. The in-process mode frames a publish through the same mapping, so a test reads the headers a live delivery carries.

The partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, rides the AMQP group-id property, and a broker that honours message groups keeps one group on one consumer. The header is named partition-key, the name the in-memory broker uses, so a service keeps its headers when it changes brokers. On publish its value becomes the message's group-id and does not travel as an application property. On delivery group-id comes back as the partition-key header. Message groups are the broker's feature. On ActiveMQ Artemis every message of one group goes to one consumer of the queue, so the consumer sees the group in the order it was sent. Competing consumers of an AmqpAddress::queue address then share the groups instead of the messages. A message type declares the header with #[outgoing(headers = ..)] and a field renamed to partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. In process the key travels as on a server, and the consumers of a queue take turns whatever the group. Pinning a group to one consumer is the server's work, so a running broker is where it shows.

request attaches a dynamic reply link, sends with reply-to and correlation-id, and resolves with the matching reply or RequestTimeout. Request-reply is part of AMQP 1.0, and AmqpPublisher implements the RequestReply capability. A request attaches a receiver link with a dynamic source, and the broker names a private address for that link. The message goes out with that address in reply-to and a fresh id in correlation-id. The call resolves with the first message on the link whose correlation-id matches, so a late answer to an earlier request is ignored. With no match inside the timeout the call returns RequestTimeout. The reply link is detached either way, so each request costs a link attach and a detach on top of the two messages. A handler asks through a slot it binds as Out<impl RequestReply>. The mount site gives the slot the plain policy: .out(DefaultSlot, Publish). The reply arrives already settled; the handler reads its payload and headers. A request that opens a conversation has no delivery to answer, so it runs from after_startup, where the publisher is already live. The other side of the exchange is a responder. Request-reply asks a pricing service for the price of each order.

A responder reads the private reply address from reply-to and answers there through an injected slot, with the request's correlation in its own AMQP type. The reply address is new for every request, so neither the reply type nor the mount site can name it. The handler reads it with ctx.headers().reply_to() and publishes with .to(reply_to) at the call site. That call site exists only for a reply type whose Outgoing derive names no destination. The slot is bound as Out<impl Publisher<Options = AmqpPublishOptions>> and mounted with .out(DefaultSlot, Publish). The answer carries the request's correlation with .correlation_id(correlation), read by Ctx(correlation): Ctx<ReplyCorrelation>. It is the request's correlation-id, or its message-id when it has none, in the type the requester wrote it: a string, binary, a UUID or a number. A Java or .NET requester often writes a UUID or a number and matches by that typed value, so the answer keeps the type rather than its text in the header map. A requester matches the answer by that id, and an answer without it never resolves the request, which then times out. A handler that answers through the reply position gets the same correlation from the Correlate transform: .out_reply(Publish).transform(Correlate), with a Ctx<ReplyCorrelation> argument on the handler. A message without reply-to is no request; the example drops it, which rejects the delivery. A request whose payload is plain bytes reads them through a Deserialized type and answers with a Serialized one, so no codec touches either side.

A handler's outcome is the delivery's disposition: ack accepts, retry sends modified with delivery-failed, drop rejects. In AMQP 1.0 a receiver settles each delivery with a disposition, and the broker acts on its outcome. ack sends accepted, and the broker forgets the message. retry sends modified with delivery-failed set and undeliverable-here cleared. The broker adds the failed attempt to the message's delivery-count and delivers it again, to this subscription or to another receiver on the address. A retry never sends released: that outcome says the delivery was not acted on, so the broker leaves the count as it was, and a cap on the attempts reads that count. drop sends rejected, which ends the delivery: the broker's dead-letter policy decides where it goes, and ActiveMQ Artemis moves it to its DLQ address by default. A delivery that is never settled, because the process stopped, stays on its link until the link detaches, and the broker then hands it to the next receiver. AMQP 1.0 has no delayed redelivery, so retry_after is the runtime's own copy. Under SettleMode::AtMostOnce the delivery is settled on receipt, and the outcome reaches no broker. In process, TestApp keeps the same rules: a retry comes back with one more counted attempt, and a drop removes the delivery. Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees settles the deliveries of a warehouse.

dead_letter(address) names the address a spent delivery is published to; a cap without one rejects it, and the broker's own dead-letter policy applies. It follows max_attempts(n) at the mount site. When the delivery that fails is the n-th one, the runtime rejects it and publishes a copy to the dead-letter address instead of the subscription's. The copy keeps the payload and the headers, and RETRY_COUNT_HEADER on it says how many times the message was delivered. It leaves through the registration's retry publisher, so the steps that follow out_retry apply to it too. The dead-letter address is an ordinary address: a subscription of this service, or of another one, reads it. A cap without dead_letter rejects the spent delivery, and a warning names the subscription. Where a rejected delivery goes is the broker's policy: ActiveMQ Artemis moves it to its DLQ address by default. The original of a dead-letter copy is rejected as well, so on Artemis the spent delivery also reaches DLQ. In process a rejected delivery leaves the transport, so a test asserts the copy on the named address, as the example's test does. Retries and dead letters reads the dead letters of a refunds service.

out_retry(Publish) replaces the registration's retry publisher, and the steps after it, such as a transform, apply to every deferred copy. The copies of a registration leave through its Retry slot. Every registration has a publisher there already, so a retry_after works with no out_retry at the mount site. out_retry names the publisher explicitly, and on this broker it is Publish, the crate's publish policy. The steps after it are the slot's steps. A PublishTransform over ForReply<C> reads the delivery being retried and edits each copy, here to add a header. It applies to every copy the registration publishes: the deferred copy, the copy an immediate retry becomes under a cap, and the dead-letter copy. The transform declares Destination = Reads: the copy goes where the runtime sends it, and a transform that declares Names does not compile on this position. The copy travels as the bytes that arrived, so no codec applies to it.

max_attempts(n) caps deliveries; the count is the broker's delivery-count, or the framework's header on a copy this crate published. The cap counts the deliveries of one message at the mount site, the first one included. A delivery whose message carries the AMQP header section reports the broker's delivery-count, which every retry increments. A message this crate published carries no header section, so the broker has counted nothing for it, and the count is RETRY_COUNT_HEADER instead. Under a cap, a retry of such a message is the runtime's copy, not the broker's redelivery: the runtime rejects the delivery and publishes it again to the subscription's address at once, with the header incremented. A delivery that reaches the cap is not retried: it goes to the dead-letter address, or is rejected where the registration names none. A retry on a registration with no cap stays the broker's own redelivery, and nothing limits it. The runtime rejects every original it replaces with a copy, so a broker that dead-letters rejected deliveries keeps those originals: ActiveMQ Artemis moves them to its DLQ address by default. The copies leave through the retry publisher of the registration. Retries and dead letters caps the attempts of a refunds service.

AMQP 1.0 has no delayed redelivery, so retry_after(delay) drops the delivery and publishes a copy to the subscription's own address after the delay. The runtime rejects the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the message, payload and headers, with RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented. The copy goes to the subscription's address, because one AMQP node is both what a receiver attaches to and what a sender publishes to, so the mount site names no destination. A bare name and every descriptor answer the same way. On a queue the copy competes for the receivers like any other message. On a topic every subscription on the address receives the copy, not only the one that asked for it. The copy waits in the service's memory, so the retry is at-most-once over the delay: a process that stops before the timer fires loses it. The rejected original is the broker's to handle: ActiveMQ Artemis moves it to its DLQ address by default, beside the copy that comes back. A cap reads the header of the copy, so it holds across delays. In a test the delay runs on the test's clock: tb.advance(delay) brings the copy back.

SettleMode::AtMostOnce settles each delivery on receipt, so the message is gone whether the handler finished or not, and ack reports Unsupported. AmqpAddress::settle sets the mode on the descriptor. SettleMode::AtLeastOnce is the default: the handler's outcome settles the delivery, as Dispositions describes. SettleMode::AtMostOnce accepts each delivery as it arrives, before the handler runs. The broker forgets the message at once, so a crash in the middle of the handler, a retry or a drop brings nothing back. The outcome the handler returns has nothing left to settle: the settlement reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning that names the subscription. The mode suits traffic where a lost message costs less than a redelivered one, such as a reading that a sensor sends again a second later. The credit of an at-most-once subscription tops itself up as the deliveries arrive. In process, TestApp settles on receipt the same way, so a test sees a retry bring nothing back.

AMQP 1.0 standardises the wire, not what an address means, so whether the subscriptions on one address compete or each get a copy is a question the broker answers. A descriptor asks the question explicitly: AmqpAddress::queue asks for competing consumers, AmqpAddress::topic for a copy each. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. It also carries the link settings: the credit, the settle mode and the deadline of a batch. The manual form passes either one to subscriber(source, body) as its first argument. The subscription's name is its address: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and a deferred retry is published back to it. A slice handler gets the deliveries assembled on the client, up to the size the mount site names, closed early by batch_wait. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. AMQP 1.0 transfers one message at a time, and credit is flow control rather than a batch size, so the subscription assembles the batches itself. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first delivery. The default, DEFAULT_BATCH_WAIT, is 10 ms. A longer wait fills batches under a trickle of traffic, at the cost of latency for the first delivery of each batch. batch_wait applies to batch handlers only: a single-message subscription hands every delivery over as it arrives. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch, and a Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles it delivery by delivery. Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees restocks a warehouse from batches.

AmqpAddress::credit sets the link credit: how many deliveries the broker may send ahead of the handler's settlements, 256 by default and never zero. AMQP 1.0 has flow control instead of a prefetch count: a receiver grants credit, and the broker sends a delivery only while it holds some. The subscription grants the full credit when it attaches. Each time half of the credit has been settled, it grants the full credit again, counted from the last delivery the broker sent. So the broker never runs more than credit deliveries ahead of the last grant, but the deliveries held unsettled can outnumber the credit. With a credit of 4, the second settlement brings four more deliveries while two are still open: six unsettled on a credit of four. The default, DEFAULT_CREDIT, is 256, and its first top-up comes after 128 settlements. On a queue, a lower credit spreads a backlog across more replicas, and a higher one keeps a fast handler busy. Under at-most-once every delivery is settled as it arrives, so the credit tops itself up without waiting for the handler. The credit is a NonZeroU32: credit(nonzero!(0)) does not compile, because a receiver with no credit receives nothing. Credit is a property of the link, which only a broker has: in process, TestApp hands every delivery over at once, and the example's live test holds the window to what a broker does.

AmqpAddress::queue asks for the queue terminus: subscriptions on the address compete, and each message goes to one of them. The descriptor attaches its receiver with the terminus capability queue on the link's source. ActiveMQ Artemis and the other brokers that read the capability treat the address as anycast. That is a work queue: two replicas of a service share the orders, and no order is handled twice. A delivery handed back with a retry goes to whichever receiver the broker picks next. Once a queue subscription has attached, the queue keeps what is published while no receiver is attached, so a replica that restarts finds its backlog. A delivery the process held unsettled when it stopped returns to the queue as well. In process, TestApp hands the messages of a queue address to its subscriptions in turn, as the example's test shows with two replicas.

AmqpAddress::raw sends the address as written with no capability, for a deployment's own convention such as /queues/orders on RabbitMQ. RabbitMQ 4.x addresses a queue by its v2 path, /queues/<name>, and ActiveMQ Artemis accepts a fully qualified queue name. A bare name in #[subscriber("orders")] is a raw address too. With no capability on the link, the broker's own configuration decides whether the subscriptions on the address compete or each get a copy. The address is matched exactly: orders and /queues/orders are two different nodes. In process, TestApp delivers each message of a raw address once, as on a queue, because there is no broker configuration to consult. A service whose subscriptions must each get a copy says topic, which is also what the brokers that need the capability have to be told.

AmqpAddress::topic asks for the topic terminus: every subscription on the address gets its own copy of each message. The descriptor attaches its receiver with the terminus capability topic on the link's source. ActiveMQ Artemis and the other brokers that read the capability treat the address as multicast. That is a broadcast: an audit trail and a notifier read the same events, each at its own pace. A deferred retry publishes its copy to the address, so every topic subscription on it receives the copy, not only the one that asked. In process, TestApp copies each message to every topic subscription of the address.

TestApp::start connects AmqpBroker in process: queues, topics, dispositions, request-reply and transactions, with no broker running. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The connected broker then carries an in-process transport in place of the connection, and so do its subscribers, its publishers and its deliveries. The descriptors and publish policies of the service are the production ones. The transport has no settings of its own. It reads the broker's URL as the connect reads it, and frames a publish with the same AMQP sections a live publish goes through, so a handler reads the headers a live delivery carries. It routes by the exact address, as a broker does. Subscriptions on a queue address compete, one delivery each, and every topic subscription gets a copy. A raw address is delivered once, like a queue; a test that asserts a broadcast subscribes with topic. A queue subscription creates its address's queue, and a message published while no consumer is attached waits there for the next one. The disposition of a handler's outcome behaves as on a broker: a retry comes back with its delivery-count one higher, a drop rejects, and an at-most-once delivery arrives settled. Batches, requests with their reply address and timeout, and transactions work as they do live. The transport refuses what a broker refuses. A message to the empty address is rejected, and a publisher, a subscription, a settlement or a transaction used after shutdown fails with the error a live connection returns. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, so the assertions that follow read finished state. What only a broker has, such as link credit, the dead-letter policy behind a rejection, message groups and the login, is for a live test. Testing an AMQP service tests a payments service in process and against a broker.

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running broker, for what only a server has: credit, dead-letter policy, grouping. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so the socket, the login and every subscription's link are real. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode covers what the in-process transport leaves to the server: link credit, the broker's dead-letter policy behind a rejection and its own delivery limit, message groups by partition key, the fan-out a broker gives a raw address, how a broker creates an address a publish reaches first, and the login. A broker keeps what earlier runs left on it. Each run reads addresses of its own, named with the process id, so it never takes a message an earlier run left behind. In the example, live::url returns the broker's URL from AMQP_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no broker. A job that stood a broker up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing URL then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is ActiveMQ Artemis in docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts on localhost:5672 with the user artemis.

AmqpTransactionalPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, posts under an AMQP transaction: what a publisher sends between begin and commit becomes visible together, or not at all. The policy needs the transaction feature. The runtime pairs it into an AmqpTxnPublisher, which implements TransactionalPublisher. A handler binds its slot as Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, and the mount site names the policy with .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish). begin_transaction declares a transaction on the broker. Each publish after it is posted under that transaction and waits for the broker's outcome, as a plain publish does. commit makes every posted message visible at once; abort discards them. A publish with no transaction open goes out at once. The handle holds one transaction at a time. A second begin_transaction while one is open fails and leaves the open one untouched. commit or abort with nothing open fails too. A commit or an abort that fails has still ended the transaction, so the next begin_transaction starts a new one. Each failure is an AmqpError::Transaction. The slot's publisher is paired once, at startup, so every delivery of the registration uses the same handle. Its one transaction serves one delivery at a time, so a registration with workers(n) opens a transaction per delivery instead, as the next section shows. A transaction covers what the publisher posts. The delivery the handler answers settles on its own after the handler returns, so a delivery redelivered after a commit posts its messages again. Transactions bills an order with its ledger entries and invoice in one transaction.

The same publisher implements OwnedTransactions. transaction() declares a transaction of its own and returns it as a value, an AmqpTransaction. The value posts with publish, and commit or abort consumes it. Any number of these are open on one publisher at a time, and settling one leaves the others whole. A registration with workers(n) uses this form: its workers share the slot's publisher, and each delivery opens its own transaction there. The handler binds its slot as Out<impl OwnedTransactions>, and the mount site names the same TransactionalPublish. A transaction dropped without commit or abort is rolled back, and a warning goes to the log.
