This guide settles deliveries, caps the attempts, reads a queue at most once, sizes the link credit and handles batches. In AMQP 1.0 a receiver settles each delivery with an outcome, and the broker acts on it. A handler's outcome is that disposition. The example is a warehouse. It picks shipments, logs every pick, and restocks its shelves from deliveries that come in batches.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Shipment { id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// The goods the warehouse has on its shelves. fn in_stock(sku: &str) -> bool { matches!(sku, "book" | "pen") } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("shipments").credit(nonzero!(32)))] async fn pick(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { if shipment.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(shipment.id, "an empty shipment rejected"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !in_stock(&shipment.sku) { tracing::info!( shipment.id, shipment.sku, "out of stock, the shipment comes back" ); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, shipment.sku, "shipment picked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { id: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// The goods the warehouse has on its shelves. fn in_stock(sku: &str) -> bool { matches!(sku, "book" | "pen") } struct Pick; impl Handle<Shipment> for Pick { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if shipment.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(shipment.id, "an empty shipment rejected"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if !in_stock(&shipment.sku) { tracing::info!( shipment.id, shipment.sku, "out of stock, the shipment comes back" ); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, shipment.sku, "shipment picked"); ready(Ok(())) } } Handler outcome Disposition What the broker does HandlerOutcome::ack() accepted removes the message HandlerOutcome::retry() modified with delivery-failed counts the attempt in delivery-count and delivers the message again HandlerOutcome::drop() rejected applies its dead-letter policy pick accepts a shipment it picked. An empty shipment can never be picked, so pick rejects it. Artemis moves a rejected message to its dead-letter address, DLQ by default. A shipment of goods that are out of stock may be picked later, so pick asks for it again. Artemis stops delivering a message after max-delivery-attempts, 10 by default, and moves it to the dead-letter address.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(pick) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .include(log_pick) .include(restock.batch(nonzero!(20usize))) }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672")) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let shipments = AmqpAddress::queue("shipments").credit(nonzero!(32)); let pick_log = AmqpAddress::queue("pick-log").settle(SettleMode::AtMostOnce); let restock = AmqpAddress::queue("restock").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(50)); b.include(subscriber(shipments, Pick).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .include(subscriber(pick_log, LogPick).build()) .include( subscriber(restock, Restocking) .batch(nonzero!(20usize)) .build(), ) }) } fn app() -> impl App { service(AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts caps the deliveries of one shipment at five, the first included. The fifth is rejected instead of asked for again. The count is the broker's delivery-count when the message carries an AMQP header section. A message this crate publishes carries none. For such a message the framework counts the attempts itself: retry publishes a copy back to shipments with a retry count in a header. Retries and dead letters adds a dead-letter address and a delay.

The subscriptions are at least once by default. A delivery the service has not settled when it stops goes back to the queue, and the next consumer gets it. So a handler may see one message twice, and its work has to tolerate that.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Picked { shipment: u64, } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("pick-log").settle(SettleMode::AtMostOnce))] async fn log_pick(picked: &Picked) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(picked.shipment, "pick logged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Picked { shipment: u64, } struct LogPick; impl Handle<Picked> for LogPick { fn handle( &self, picked: &Picked, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(picked.shipment, "pick logged"); ready(Ok(())) } } SettleMode::AtMostOnce settles each delivery on receipt. The broker forgets the message the moment it hands it over, so a crash before the handler finishes loses it. That suits the pick log, where a missing line costs less than a second pass over the broker. The handler's outcome has nothing left to settle: ack and nack report AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning for each.

.credit(nonzero!(32)) on shipments is the link credit: how many deliveries the broker may send ahead of the service's settlements. The default is DEFAULT_CREDIT, 256. Once half of the credit is settled, the client grants the full credit again. A slow handler therefore holds the broker back instead of filling the service's memory, and the rest of the queue stays on the broker for the other replicas. The credit is a NonZeroU32, because a link with no credit receives nothing: credit(nonzero!(0)) does not compile.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Restock { sku: String, quantity: u32, } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("restock").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(50)))] async fn restock(items: &[Restock]) -> HandlerOutcome { let units: u32 = items.iter().map(|item| item.quantity).sum(); tracing::info!(lines = items.len(), units, "shelves restocked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Restock { sku: String, quantity: u32, } struct Restocking; impl Handle<[Restock]> for Restocking { fn handle( &self, items: &[Restock], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let units: u32 = items.iter().map(|item| item.quantity).sum(); tracing::info!(lines = items.len(), units, "shelves restocked"); ready(Ok(())) } } A handler that takes a slice gets a batch, and .batch(nonzero!(20usize)) at the mount site sets its largest size. AMQP 1.0 transfers one message at a time, so the batch is put together on the client. A batch holds at most 20 deliveries, and fewer when no more arrived in time. batch_wait is how long a partial batch waits for more, 50 milliseconds here and 10 by default. The outcome of restock settles every delivery of the batch.

The tests in the example file run the warehouse in process. They check each outcome, the five deliveries of a shipment out of stock, the pick log and the batches. Credit, the broker's dead-letter policy and its delivery limit belong to Artemis, so the in-process broker leaves them out. Testing an AMQP service covers the harness.
This guide installs ruststream-amqp, starts a local AMQP 1.0 broker and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-amqp = "0.8" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-amqp = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-amqp is the AMQP 1.0 broker. Its testing feature adds the in-process broker that tests run on. The broker crate has these features, all off by default: Feature What it gives rustls amqps:// connections over TLS with rustls native-tls amqps:// connections over the platform's TLS transaction transactional publishing asyncapi the AMQP 1.0 details in the generated AsyncAPI document testing the in-process broker behind TestApp The client underneath is fe2o3-amqp, written in Rust, so the build needs no system libraries.

One ActiveMQ Artemis is enough to develop against: compose.yaml services: artemis: image: apache/activemq-artemis:latest-alpine environment: ARTEMIS_USER: artemis ARTEMIS_PASSWORD: artemis ports: - "5672:5672" docker compose up -d The broker listens for AMQP on localhost:5672, with the user artemis and the password artemis. Artemis creates a queue the first time a service reads it, so there is nothing to declare.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| b.include(take_order), ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| b.include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), TakeOrder).build()), ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the queue orders. It accepts an order with an amount and rejects one without. AmqpAddress::queue names the queue, and Queues and topics shows the other kinds of address. AmqpBroker::new takes the broker's URL and only records it. The connection opens when the service starts. The user and password in the URL log the service in. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish an order from another terminal with the command-line client that ships in the image: docker compose exec artemis /opt/activemq-artemis/bin/artemis producer \ --protocol amqp --user artemis --password artemis \ --destination queue://orders --message-count 1 --message '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. AmqpBroker connects to an in-process broker there, so the tests need no Artemis: cargo test Testing an AMQP service walks through such tests and what the in-process broker models.

A service on fe2o3-amqp opens its connection and sessions, attaches its links and writes a receive loop. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: fe2o3-amqp RustStream Connection::open AmqpBroker::new, with sasl and container_id Session::begin nothing: each subscription gets a session of its own, and the publishers share one Receiver::attach and a recv loop a #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::..)] handler CreditMode::Auto(n) AmqpAddress::credit accept, modify, reject the handler's outcome: ack, retry, drop (Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees) auto_accept(true) SettleMode::AtMostOnce Sender::attach and send a reply or an Out parameter, sent through the Publish policy a dynamic receiver for replies request (Requests and replies) Controller and Transaction::declare TransactionalPublish (Publishing all or nothing) A service that speaks AMQP 0.9.1 to RabbitMQ uses ruststream-lapin instead: the two protocols share the port and the amqp:// scheme, and they are different protocols.
A production broker asks for TLS and credentials, and its operators look for a service by name.

src/main.rs /// Where the broker is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Endpoint { url: String, username: String, password: String, } impl Endpoint { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); Self { url: read("AMQP_URL"), username: read("AMQP_USERNAME"), password: read("AMQP_PASSWORD"), } } } fn broker(endpoint: Endpoint) -> AmqpBroker { AmqpBroker::new(endpoint.url) .sasl(Sasl::plain(endpoint.username, endpoint.password)) .container_id("orders-eu-1") } Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-amqp = { version = "0.8", features = ["rustls"] } The deployment provides the address and the credentials in environment variables. An amqps:// URL connects over TLS. It names the broker by a host name or an IPv4 address: TLS checks that name against the broker's certificate. An IPv6 address gives TLS no server name, so the connect fails on it. TLS needs one of two features: rustls uses rustls, and native-tls uses the platform's TLS. Sasl::plain logs the service in with a user name and a password. The URL then carries no credentials. A password with characters that have a meaning in a URL, such as /, ? or @, goes through Sasl::plain as it is. Sasl::anonymous connects without credentials. Sasl::external logs in with the client certificate set by AmqpBroker::tls, as the security page shows. On Azure Service Bus the user name is the name of a shared access policy and the password is its key, as its AMQP guide describes.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker(Endpoint::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: AmqpBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }) } fn app() -> impl App { service(broker(Endpoint::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } container_id names the service to the broker, ruststream by default. The broker's console lists the connection under that name, and the links of the service are named after it. Give each deployment of a service its own container id, so an operator tells them apart. Each subscription runs on an AMQP session of its own, and the publishers share one more. Flow control works per session, so a slow consumer does not hold back the publishers or another subscription.

When the service stops, it closes the connection from the inside out: the subscriptions' sessions, the publishers' links and their session, then the connection. A publisher used after that reports AmqpError::NotConnected instead of succeeding against a closed connection. The AsyncAPI document of the service names the broker's host and port and never the credentials.

The tests start the production service with the production broker, given test credentials, under TestApp::start. The in-process broker checks the URL the way the client reads it, without dialling the broker. A URL the client cannot open fails the start: the scheme "https" is not an AMQP scheme The tests need the same TLS feature as the service: without it, an amqps:// URL fails the start too. Authentication and the certificate check happen only on a real broker.

This guide reads a work queue, broadcasts on a topic, keeps a broadcast for a reader that is away, and publishes to an address. AMQP 1.0 fixes the wire and leaves the meaning of an address to the broker. A subscription therefore says what it wants: AmqpAddress has a constructor for each intent, and the link tells the broker which one it is. What this page states is proved against ActiveMQ Artemis, the broker the crate's tests run on. The example is an orders service. It takes orders from a queue and announces each taken order on a topic, which billing, an audit log and a ledger follow.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// What every service that follows orders hears about a taken order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "order-events")] struct OrderTaken { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), reply)] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> OrderTaken { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); OrderTaken { order: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// What every service that follows orders hears about a taken order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderTaken { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for OrderTaken { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "order-events"; } impl MessageHeaders for OrderTaken { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for OrderTaken { const NAME: &'static str = "OrderTaken"; } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order, OrderTaken> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderTaken, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); ready(Ok(OrderTaken { order: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, })) } } AmqpAddress::queue asks for a queue: the link carries the terminus capability queue. Artemis then creates an anycast address orders with one queue behind it. Consumers on a queue compete, and each order goes to one of them. To take orders faster, run more replicas of the service: each replica is one more consumer of orders. take_order answers each order with an OrderTaken. OrderTaken names its address with #[outgoing(name = "order-events")], so the bare reply clause sends it there.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::topic("order-events"))] async fn bill(event: &OrderTaken) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order, event.amount_cents, "invoice issued"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::topic("order-events"))] async fn audit(event: &OrderTaken) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order, "order recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<OrderTaken> for Bill { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderTaken, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order, event.amount_cents, "invoice issued"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderTaken> for Audit { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderTaken, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order, "order recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } AmqpAddress::topic asks for a topic: the link carries the capability topic. Artemis makes order-events a multicast address and gives each subscription a queue of its own. So bill and audit each get a copy of every OrderTaken. A topic subscription lives as long as its link. What is published to order-events while the service is down is not kept for it. A reader that must not miss a message reads a queue.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Reads the queue `ledger` that the operator created on the `order-events` address. #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::raw("order-events::ledger"))] async fn post_to_ledger(event: &OrderTaken) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order, "order posted to the ledger"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Reads the queue `ledger` that the operator created on the `order-events` address. struct PostToLedger; impl Handle<OrderTaken> for PostToLedger { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderTaken, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order, "order posted to the ledger"); ready(Ok(())) } } The ledger must see every order, also the ones taken while it was stopped. The operator creates a durable queue ledger on the multicast address order-events: docker compose exec artemis /opt/activemq-artemis/bin/artemis queue create \ --user artemis --password artemis --silent \ --name ledger --address order-events --auto-create-address \ --multicast --durable --preserve-on-no-consumers Every message published to order-events now lands in ledger too, whether post_to_ledger runs or not. order-events::ledger is the queue's fully qualified name in Artemis: the address, two colons, the queue. AmqpAddress::raw sends an address as written, with no capability, so the link attaches to that queue. A bare #[subscriber("order-events::ledger")] does the same.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(take_order) .out_reply(Publish) .include(bill) .include(audit) .include(post_to_ledger) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { let ledger = AmqpAddress::raw("order-events::ledger"); b.include( subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), TakeOrder) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::topic("order-events"), Bill).build()) .include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::topic("order-events"), Audit).build()) .include(subscriber(ledger, PostToLedger).build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } .out_reply(Publish) names the publisher of the replies, AmqpPublish under its prelude name. A publish attaches a sender link to the reply's address on first use and keeps it. A message the broker refuses fails the publish with AmqpError::PublishNotAccepted.

The well-known headers travel in the AMQP properties section: content-type, correlation-id, reply-to, message-id. Every other header travels in application-properties. A message from this crate is a plain AMQP message, so a client in another language reads it without RustStream. The partition key travels as the PARTITION_KEY_HEADER header and becomes the message's group-id. Artemis uses group-id for message grouping: every message of one group goes to the same consumer of a queue. So orders keyed by customer keep their order across replicas.
Other brokers name their nodes their own way, and raw passes their spelling as it is. Their own documentation describes it: RabbitMQ 4.x, Azure Service Bus, ActiveMQ Classic, which Amazon MQ runs.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. One order publishes one OrderTaken, orders is called once, and order-events is called twice, once for each topic subscription. The in-process broker delivers a raw address exactly as written, so its test publishes to order-events::ledger directly. Testing an AMQP service covers the harness.

This guide asks another service over AMQP 1.0 and waits for its answer, answers requests on their reply address, and handles a request nobody answers. Request-reply is part of the protocol. A request carries a reply address in reply-to and an id in correlation-id. The answer goes to that address and repeats that id. The example is two services in one app. The pricing service answers questions about prices, and the orders service asks it for the price of each order.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// What the orders service asks the pricing service. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Ask { sku: String, } /// The pricing service's answer, sent to the reply address of the request. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Price { sku: String, cents: u64, } /// The catalogue the pricing service answers from. fn price_of(sku: &str) -> Option<u64> { match sku { "book" => Some(1250), "pen" => Some(150), _ => None, } } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Price)] struct Answers; #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("prices.quote"))] async fn quote( ask: &Ask, ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, Ctx(correlation): Ctx<ReplyCorrelation>, Out(answers): Out<impl Publisher<Options = AmqpPublishOptions>, Answers>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Some(reply_to) = ctx.headers().reply_to().map(str::to_owned) else { tracing::warn!(ask.sku, "a question without a reply address dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let Some(cents) = price_of(&ask.sku) else { tracing::info!(ask.sku, "no price for the item, no answer"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let price = Price { sku: ask.sku.clone(), cents, }; if answers .message(&price) .to(reply_to) // The requester matches the answer to its question by the correlation id, in the type // it wrote the id in. .correlation_id(correlation) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// What the orders service asks the pricing service. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Ask { sku: String, } /// The pricing service's answer, sent to the reply address of the request. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Price { sku: String, cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Price { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Price { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Price { const NAME: &'static str = "Price"; } /// The catalogue the pricing service answers from. fn price_of(sku: &str) -> Option<u64> { match sku { "book" => Some(1250), "pen" => Some(150), _ => None, } } struct Answers; impl OutSlot for Answers { const NAME: &'static str = "Answers"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Answers> for Price {} struct Quote; impl<Sent> Handle<Ask, (), Outs<(Sent,)>, AmqpContext> for Quote where Sent: OutEntry<Answers, Wire: Publisher<Options = AmqpPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, ask: &Ask, outs: &Outs<(Sent,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Some(reply_to) = ctx.headers().reply_to().map(str::to_owned) else { tracing::warn!(ask.sku, "a question without a reply address dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let Some(cents) = price_of(&ask.sku) else { tracing::info!(ask.sku, "no price for the item, no answer"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; // The requester matches the answer to its question by the correlation id, in the type // it wrote the id in. let correlation = ctx.context(ReplyCorrelation).cloned(); let price = Price { sku: ask.sku.clone(), cents, }; if outs .get(Answers) .message(&price) .to(reply_to) .correlation_id(correlation) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } A request arrives at a responder with its reply address in the reply-to header, and ctx.headers().reply_to() reads it. quote publishes the price through its Answers slot with to(reply_to), because the address is new for every request. Price therefore declares no address of its own. The answer carries the request's correlation-id in the type the requester wrote it, read by Ctx<ReplyCorrelation> and set with .correlation_id(..), and the requester takes only an answer whose id matches. An item without a price gets no answer, and the requester's timeout ends the wait. The responder reads the queue prices.quote. Each replica of the pricing service is one more consumer of it, and each request goes to one of them.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long the orders service waits for a price. const PRICING_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// How long an order waits before it asks for its price again. const RETRY_DELAY: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); }; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("prices.quote", ask.as_slice()); let reply = match outs.get(Pricing).request(request, PRICING_TIMEOUT).await { Ok(reply) => reply, Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "no price, the order asks again later"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RETRY_DELAY)); } }; let Ok(price) = serde_json::from_slice::<Price>(reply.payload()) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; tracing::info!(order.id, price.cents, "order priced"); The Pricing slot is bounded Out<impl RequestReply, _>: the body says it needs request-reply and names no broker. The app pairs the slot with the plain Publish policy, whose publisher, AmqpPublisher, carries request-reply. request attaches a dynamic receiver link, so the broker creates a private reply address for this one request. It publishes the question with reply-to and correlation-id set and resolves with the first matching answer. ActiveMQ Artemis backs a dynamic link with a temporary queue. The question is a raw message, so the body encodes it and decodes the answer itself, here with serde_json. The order's reply, Priced, goes out once the price is known. A request nobody answers fails after its timeout, two seconds here, with AmqpError::RequestTimeout. The reply link is detached either way. The order then waits 30 seconds on its queue and asks again.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(quote) .out(Answers, Publish) .include(price_order) .out_reply(Publish) .out(Pricing, Publish) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("prices.quote"), Quote).build()) .out(Answers, Publish) .include( subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("orders"), PriceOrder) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .out(Pricing, Publish) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Both slots take the plain Publish policy: one publishes answers, the other asks questions. A request that starts a conversation has no delivery to answer. It runs from a startup hook, a step of the mount chain before the includes: b.after_startup(Publish, ..).include(..), with request on the publisher the hook is handed. The tests in the example file run both halves in one app in process. The in-process broker routes a request to the app's own responder, matches the answer by its correlation id, and times a silent responder out.

This guide retries a delivery now or later, caps the attempts, moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter address and marks the copies. AMQP 1.0 has no delayed redelivery, and a link cannot declare a delivery limit or a dead-letter address. The framework covers both: the mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter address, and a delayed retry travels as a copy of the message with a retry count in a header. The example is a refunds service that sends refunds through a card processor.

The processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means it takes no more large refunds for now: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means the card's bank did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("refunds"))] async fn process_refund(refund: &Refund) -> HandlerOutcome { match send_refund(refund) { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Refund { const NAME: &'static str = "Refund"; } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund> for ProcessRefund { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(match send_refund(refund) { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } }) } } retry_after settles the delivery and publishes a copy to refunds once the delay has passed. The copy carries the retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. The delayed copy is at most once: a process that stops before the delay ends loses it. On a queue the copy goes to one consumer like any other message.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter address. b.include(process_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dead") .out_retry(Publish) .transform(Retried) .include(review) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( AmqpBroker::new("amqp://artemis:artemis@localhost:5672"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter address. b.include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("refunds"), ProcessRefund).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dead") .out_retry(Publish) .transform(Retried) .include(subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("refunds.dead"), Review).build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one refund, the first included. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to refunds.dead, payload and headers as they arrived. A dropped refund is rejected and goes to the broker's own dead-letter policy, not to refunds.dead. Under a cap the framework reads the count from the delivery. It is the broker's delivery-count when the message carries an AMQP header section. A message published by this crate carries none, so retry then publishes a copy at once, and the retry-count header counts the attempts. A cap without dead_letter rejects the last delivery instead, and the broker's dead-letter policy decides. The broker also has a limit of its own: Artemis stops after max-delivery-attempts, 10 by default. Choose one owner for the limit: a cap below the broker's limit makes the framework's count the one that applies.

The retry-count header of a dead letter holds the number of deliveries it went through, 5 here. review reads it with ctx.headers() and logs the refund for a person to look at.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Marks every copy with the address its delivery came from. #[derive(Clone)] struct Retried; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for Retried { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } src/main.rs /// Marks every copy with the address its delivery came from. #[derive(Clone)] struct Retried; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for Retried { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } A copy has no call site in the handler, so a publish transform is the one place that reaches it. The app mounts process_refund with .out_retry(Publish).transform(Retried). .out_retry(Publish) names the publisher of the copies, and the steps after it apply to them. Retried writes the address the delivery came from into x-retried-from. Every copy goes back to the address of its subscription, so a transform on this position may not change the destination.

A copy is published to the subscription's own address. On a topic address that address is shared, so every subscription on the topic gets the copy, not only the one that asked for it. Retry on a queue when one reader owns the message.
The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. Testing an AMQP service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process broker or against a running one. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on the queue card-payments, and the handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without a card is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments.review, the dead-letter address. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker's URL and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-amqp in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(AmqpBroker::new(URL))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb, 1).await } // Start and shutdown are cold steps whose futures carry no `Send`; the test awaits them on // its own runtime. #[allow(clippy::future_not_send)] async fn a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt( tb: TestApp<()>, id: u64, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .message(&payment(id, 2_500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: id, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(AmqpBroker::new(URL))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb, 1).await } // Start and shutdown are cold steps whose futures carry no `Send`; the test awaits them on // its own runtime. #[allow(clippy::future_not_send)] async fn a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt( tb: TestApp<()>, id: u64, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .message(&payment(id, 2_500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: id, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects AmqpBroker to an in-process broker. The broker's URL is never dialled. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<AmqpBroker>(). publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app and the payment's id as arguments, so the live test below runs it too.

A minute of HOLD costs nothing. AMQP 1.0 has no delayed redelivery, so retry_after publishes a copy of the payment to its queue when the delay ends. The copy carries the retry count in a header, and published shows it on card-payments next to the test's own message. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the payment goes to card-payments.review, the dead-letter address, as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: The in-process broker reads the broker's URL the way connect does. A URL the client cannot open fails the test's start, and amqps:// needs the rustls or native-tls feature there too. A publish is turned into an AMQP message and back, so a handler reads the headers a live delivery carries. It models the broker's routing: Consumers of a queue address compete, one delivery each; every topic subscription gets a copy. A raw address is delivered exactly as written, to one consumer. A queue subscription creates its queue, and the queue keeps what arrives while no consumer is attached. retry counts the attempt in delivery-count, and a delivery left unsettled goes back to the queue when its subscription ends. An at-most-once subscription gets its deliveries settled, and ack reports AckError::Unsupported. A transaction publishes nothing before its commit, and a request times out when nothing answers. Link credit, the broker's dead-letter policy and delivery limit, durability, and the addresses a broker creates for a publish need a running broker. In process, a message to an address that no queue subscription has opened is dropped.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_from_a_broker() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("AMQP_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(AmqpBroker::new(url))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb, u64::from(process::id())).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_from_a_broker() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("AMQP_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(AmqpBroker::new(url))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb, u64::from(process::id())).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running broker. The test reads the URL from AMQP_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. The payment's id is the process id, so the messages of one run are told apart on the broker. documents.t: This guide publishes several messages from one handler together or not at all. AMQP 1.0 has transactions in the protocol: a sender posts messages inside a transaction, and the broker makes them visible on the commit. The transaction feature turns this on: Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-amqp = { version = "0.8", features = ["transaction"] } The example is a billing service. It turns each order into ledger entries and an invoice, and either all of them reach the broker or none does.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "billing.orders")] struct Order { id: u64, lines: Vec<Line>, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Line { sku: String, cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "ledger")] struct LedgerEntry { order: u64, sku: String, cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices")] struct Invoice { order: u64, total_cents: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(LedgerEntry, Invoice)] struct Billing; #[subscriber(AmqpAddress::queue("billing.orders"))] async fn bill( order: &Order, Out(billing): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Billing>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if billing.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for line in &order.lines { if line.cents == 0 { tracing::warn!( order.id, line.sku, "a line without a price, nothing is billed" ); // A failed abort has still ended the transaction, so there is nothing left to undo. let _ = billing.abort().await; return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } let entry = LedgerEntry { order: order.id, sku: line.sku.clone(), cents: line.cents, }; if billing.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { let _ = billing.abort().await; return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } let invoice = Invoice { order: order.id, total_cents: order.lines.iter().map(|line| line.cents).sum(), }; if billing.message(&invoice).publish().await.is_err() { let _ = billing.abort().await; return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if billing.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, invoice.total_cents, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, lines: Vec<Line>, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Billing> for LedgerEntry {} impl PublishedThrough<Billing> for Invoice {} struct Bill; impl<Sent> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Sent,)>> for Bill where Sent: OutEntry<Billing, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Sent,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let billing = outs.get(Billing); if billing.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for line in &order.lines { if line.cents == 0 { tracing::warn!( order.id, line.sku, "a line without a price, nothing is billed" ); // A failed abort has still ended the transaction, so there is nothing left to undo. let _ = billing.abort().await; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let entry = LedgerEntry { order: order.id, sku: line.sku.clone(), cents: line.cents, }; if billing.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { let _ = billing.abort().await; return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } let invoice = Invoice { order: order.id, total_cents: order.lines.iter().map(|line| line.cents).sum(), }; if billing.message(&invoice).publish().await.is_err() { let _ = billing.abort().await; return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if billing.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(order.id, invoice.total_cents, "order billed"); Ok(()) } } The Billing slot is bounded Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, _>: the body says it needs transactions and names no broker. begin_transaction opens a transaction on the slot's publisher. Every publish after it is posted inside the transaction, and the broker holds it back. commit makes the ledger entries and the invoice visible together. A line without a price makes the order unbillable, and abort discards what was posted, so nothing reaches ledger or invoices. A commit or an abort that fails has still ended the transaction, so the next begin_transaction starts a fresh one. bill retries the order when the commit fails.

Its publisher holds one transaction at a time. A second begin_transaction while one is open returns an error and leaves the open one untouched. Each registration gets a publisher of its own, so two handlers can each hold a transaction at the same time. A publish on this publisher outside a transaction goes out at once. A handler with workers(n) shares one publisher among its workers, so each delivery opens a transaction of its own with transaction(), as Transactions shows. A transaction that starts the service, with no delivery to handle, runs from a startup hook. The hook is a step of the mount chain written before the includes: b.after_startup(TransactionalPublish, ..).include(..) hands it the same publisher.

The transaction covers what the handler publishes. The order's delivery is settled after the handler returns, outside the transaction. A crash between the commit and the settlement delivers the order again, and its ledger entries and invoice are published a second time. Give the messages an id the readers can use to drop a repeat, such as the order's id here.
